extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the USPTO (trademark attorneys), counsel subject to USPTO discipline, and OED practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements governing trademark practitioners' conduct before the USPTO, including electronic signature rules, supervisory duties over non-practitioner assistants, duties to clients and the tribunal, and rules governing affidavit(s) of resignation and reinstatement. Focused on compliance with the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct and related trademark filing procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic signature requirements for trademark filings (37 C.F.R. § 2.193; TMEP § 611.01)
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO regulations require that the person named as the signatory on an electronic trademark document filed with the Office must personally enter his or her electronic signature on the document (i.e., personally enter the combination of letters, numbers, spaces and/or punctuation marks adopted as a signature, placed between two forward slash ("/") symbols in the signature block on the electronic submission). See 37 C.F.R. § 2.193(a)(2), (c), and (e); TMEP § 611.01(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All documents must be personally signed. The person(s) identified as the signatory must manually enter the elements of the electronic signature. Another person (e.g., paralegal, legal assistant, or secretary) may not sign the name of a qualified practitioner or other authorized signatory. Typing the electronic signature of another person is not a valid signature. The signature block must use the forward-slash format. This requirement is critical to filing integrity and the validity of declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of signature integrity and declaration warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark documents filed with the Office—such as Trademark/Service Mark Statements of Use—typically carry an important warning in the declarations about willful false statements under 18 U.S.C. § 1001 and possible jeopardy to the application or registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must appreciate that declarations warn that willful false statements are punishable by fine or imprisonment (18 U.S.C. § 1001) and may jeopardize the validity of the application/registration. Because of the legal risks, electronic signatures must be personally made by the named signatory to preserve the integrity of the filing and avoid criminal/civil consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner competence, diligence, and client communication (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.101, 11.103, 11.104(a)(3), 11.104(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must provide competent representation, act with reasonable diligence and promptness, keep the client reasonably informed about the status of a matter, and explain matters to the extent reasonably necessary to allow the client to make informed decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence includes understanding applicable USPTO rules (e.g., signature rules); diligence includes timely, proactive investigation and corrective action when issues arise; communication includes informing clients about filing status and material risks (including risks from improper signature practices) and explaining consequences sufficiently for informed client decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties regarding false statements and remedial measures (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1), (a)(3), (b), (d))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must not make false statements of fact or law to the USPTO and must correct false statements of material fact or law previously made. If the practitioner knows of falsity in material evidence offered, the practitioner must take reasonable remedial measures, including, if necessary, disclosure to the tribunal. In ex parte proceedings, the practitioner must inform the tribunal of all material facts known that will enable an informed decision, whether or not the facts are adverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obligations include active correction of prior filings, disclosure to the tribunal when required, and comprehensive disclosure of material facts in ex parte matters. Failure to correct or disclose can constitute professional misconduct and may trigger disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervisory responsibilities over non-practitioner assistants (37 C.F.R. § 11.503(b), 11.503(c)(1), 11.503(c)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner having direct supervisory authority over a non-practitioner assistant must make reasonable efforts to ensure that the non-practitioner's conduct is compatible with the professional obligations of the practitioner. A practitioner with knowledge of improper conduct may not order or ratify that conduct and must take reasonable remedial action when the conduct of non-practitioner assistants under the practitioner's supervision violates the Rules, if the practitioner knows of the conduct at a time when its consequences can be avoided or mitigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable efforts include training, oversight, and verification (e.g., ensuring signatories personally enter signatures). If a supervised assistant engages in impermissible conduct (such as entering a practitioner's electronic signature), the practitioner must act promptly to prevent, mitigate, and remediate consequences, and must not authorize or acquiesce in the conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to notify affected clients and USPTO when impermissible signatures discovered
rubrics_metrics.description: When a practitioner's name was entered on filings by someone else (e.g., non-practitioner assistants or third parties), the practitioner has a duty to contact applicants/clients to inform them that the named signatory did not personally sign declarations and to inform them of actual or potential adverse consequences of non-compliance with signature rules. The practitioner also should contact Trademark Operations at the USPTO as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedial steps include notifying clients of the impermissible signatures and potential jeopardy to rights, inquiring whether third parties have contacted clients, and notifying USPTO Trademark Operations where necessary to address and correct filings. Failure to notify clients or USPTO may be cited as aggravating conduct in disciplinary proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proscribed misconduct definitions (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c), (d), (i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation; conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice; and other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the USPTO are proscribed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions such as permitting false declarations, allowing others to sign on the practitioner's behalf, ordering or ratifying improper conduct, or failing to remediate known falsities may constitute these forms of proscribed conduct and lead to exclusion or other discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for affidavit of resignation and exclusion on consent (37 C.F.R. § 11.27(a), (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: An Affidavit of Resignation Pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.27 must be freely and voluntarily rendered, demonstrate awareness of pending disciplinary allegations and the consequences of consenting to exclusion, and comply with the regulatory requirements of § 11.27(a) for approval by the USPTO Director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The affidavit must acknowledge voluntariness, awareness of the disciplinary complaint, and understanding of the legal and factual consequences of consenting to exclusion. The Director reviews and may approve the affidavit; upon approval the practitioner is excluded on consent from practice before the Office in the specified matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumptions upon reinstatement (37 C.F.R. § 11.60) and consequences for applications for reinstatement
rubrics_metrics.description: If and when a practitioner who consented to exclusion applies for reinstatement under 37 C.F.R. § 11.60, the OED Director may conclusively presume, for purposes of the reinstatement determination, that the allegations in the underlying disciplinary complaint are true and that the practitioner could not have successfully defended against them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners consenting to exclusion should understand that future reinstatement proceedings may operate under presumptions adverse to them; this affects documentation, disclosures, and the burden during a reinstatement application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural publication and notice requirements following exclusion on consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Following approval of an affidavit of resignation and exclusion on consent, the OED Director shall electronically publish the Final Order in the Office of Enrollment and Discipline's FOIA Reading Room and publish a materially consistent notice in the Official Gazette.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusion on consent is publicly disclosed via the OED FOIA Reading Room and the Official Gazette; practitioners should expect public notice of disciplinary outcomes and the content specified by the Office (e.g., factual summary and legal basis).
